item.title: Fed chair warns AI spending could fuel inflation and pledges to contain prices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned of a potential "shock" to the U.S. economy delivered by a rise in artificial intelligence spending , pledging to contain price increases as a flood of private sector funds drives up demand. "If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognize this as a shock," Warsh said in Bangkok, Thailand, at a conference organized by the International Monetary Fund. A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters. In theory, an onrush of investment in activities like chip manufacturing and data center construction could put upward pressure in general on consumer prices, unless the demand is offset by a new supply of goods and services. Which grocery prices are rising the fastest and which are falling? "It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s hitting the supply side of the economy," Warsh said. Warsh, who took the helm of the Fed in May, has previously weighed in on the potential impact of AI on the labor market and wider economy. On Friday, Warsh reiterated his optimism about AI, saying the technology would ultimately generate added productivity and wealth. But, Warsh added, "the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one." "We really don’t know what the market structure will be of these new technologies," Warsh said. "Who's going to be making the money?" Warsh acknowledged other shocks faced by the U.S. economy, including "shocks of war and military conflict." Eli Hartman/Bloomberg via Getty Images - PHOTO: The Nscale data center project in Barstow, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. The outbreak of the Iran war in February imposed a historic oil supply shock and caused an acceleration of price increases in many countries. A U.S. government report issued this week showed inflation had climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Middle East conflict continued to drive up gasoline prices. Prices rose 3.7% in September, according to new data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics . Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Fed's target rate of 2%. "It’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said on Friday. He later added: "I’ve heard resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability. I’ve certainly delivered that resolve." Price hikes prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point in September, marking the central bank's first rate increase since 2023. An increase to the benchmark interest rate aims to slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months. The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections. Gas prices set record for highest number of days above $4 a gallon in a calendar year Consistent with his approach in previous public appearances, Warsh opted against issuing a forecast about what the central bank may do at its meeting later this month. "I don’t pre-judge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have over the balance of this year," Warsh said. Many investors appeared to interpret Warsh's posture as a sign the Fed may hold interest rates steady later this month. As of Friday morning, investors peg the chance of the Fed maintaining current interest rates at about 86%, which marks an uptick from about 55% on Wednesday, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool , a measure of market sentiment. item.title: 'You should be ashamed of yourself': Heated Senate debates become personal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WCSH Candidates faced off in heated debates Thursday night in two of the country’s most competitive Senate races , showing how bitter — and personal — each contest has become. In Maine, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson told GOP Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” after she suggested a protester was one of his supporters. And in Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan questioned Democratic opponent Mary Peltola’s “character” while citing allegations she mistreated staff. “I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and dishonesty,” Peltola said during another exchange. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself.” The races are unfolding thousands of miles apart but both critical to the Senate majority. Collins, a moderate Republican, is seeking reelection in a blue state, while Sullivan is running for another term in more GOP-leaning Alaska where Peltola, a former congresswoman, is well-known. Both debates showed how much of a political liability President Donald Trump’s war in Iran has become for Republican incumbents. Sullivan said it “needs to end soon,” while Collins continued to insist Trump should have consulted Congress on the conflict. Here’s a look at key moments from the debates. US Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate for the US Senate Troy Jackson are seen during their debate at the Gracie Theatre in Bangor, Maine on Thursday. - Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images A protester disrupts Collins on data centers The fourth and final Senate debate in Maine grew heated as Collins and Jackson sharpened their attacks. Within minutes, a protester shouted at Collins about the impact of data centers, forcing the debate to a brief halt. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our waters,” the protester yelled. Following the incident, Collins said the protester “is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” “Oh, shut up,” Jackson replied, saying he did not know who the person was. unknown content item - Corruption allegations and campaign financing in Maine During the Collins-Jackson debate, both candidates tried to portray their opponent as corrupt, a major theme that has loomed over the hotly contested race and the midterms nationally. Collins cornered Jackson for not sharing his FEC report with her on Wednesday, a promise he made at their debate earlier this week. Jackson said he missed his self-imposed deadline because it took longer to process the donations from 200,000 people to his campaign than he expected. “I had to make sure this report was right. It was my first one,” Jackson said. Throughout the campaign, Jackson has framed Collins as being influenced by her donors and touted that he doesn’t take any corporate PAC money. Collins tried to flip the script on Thursday by dinging Jackson for running joint ads with his party’s Senate campaign arm, which does take money from corporations, and for not disclosing his donors. Jackson said he did not control their donations to the Senate campaign committee but did concede his campaign has taken money from billionaires. “That is accurate. But I haven’t made any deals like Senator Collins has with those billionaires. I don’t owe them any votes. I am going to tax those billionaires when I get to the US Senate. So, if they want to give me money during this campaign, I guess that’s up to them,” Jackson said. When it was Jackson’s turn to ask Collins a question, he got personal. In defending his credentials and pushing back on Collins’ critique that he doesn’t have the right experience, Jackson exclaimed, “Is it just me that you look down on or is it working-class people overall?” Collins further distances from Trump on Iran war Collins doubled down on her criticism of the Iran war as the Maine Republican continues to distance herself from Trump. When asked if Congress should have been consulted before Trump decided to go to war, Collins said, “Congress definitely should have been consulted.” But Collins added that that the War Powers Resolution gave Trump the flexibility to act unilaterally within the first 60 days of the conflict, which she said is why she did not start voting to rein in Trump’s war powers until after those initial 60 days had passed. unknown content item - Iran war’s consequences also hangs over Alaska debate Sullivan repeatedly had to grapple with issues where Trump has not made the race easy for him. The war in Iran, for example, has led to especially high fuel costs in Alaska. Sullivan said he has opposed limiting Trump’s Iran powers because he supports the overall goal of preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he said the war “needs to end soon.” “The energy costs from this war are too high, but … the best way to bring down costs with regard to energy in Alaska is to produce more energy by and for Alaskans,” Sullivan said, suggesting Peltola could not be trusted to support that. Peltola blamed Washington politicians for “waging forever wars that are skyrocketing our costs.” And she scoffed at Sullivan’s pivot to the topic of domestic energy production. “I have been a strong supporter of drilling in Alaska,” she said. “That is not the issue here.” Sullivan continued to show daylight with Trump when asked about Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel . He reiterated his opposition, saying, “I don’t think it’s a good ideal at all,” and noting he “just led the effort” to pass new sanctions on Russia in Congress. Sullivan, Peltola spar over her treatment of staff Sullivan and Peltola clashed twice over a September story from The New York Times that alleged staff mistreatment by Peltola. In the article, her campaign pushed back on the suggestion she regularly abused her staff but said she occasionally “struggled to deal with her grief” after her mother and husband died in 2023. “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” Peltola said at the debate when asked about the Times report. Sullivan emphasized that the story was based on interviews with nine former staff members and at least 20 other people. “It’s not Mary Peltola on her worst day,” Sullivan said. “It’s Mary Peltola over the course of a couple years with dozens of people weighing in on this.” Sullivan brought up the Times story on his own earlier in the debate, saying Peltola has “treated young Alaskans horribly” and that it was “a character flaw.” Peltola called it “gossip” and “unfounded allegations” as Sullivan talked over her. “It’s the New York Times,” he said. “Read the article.” Sullivan questions whether Peltola got questions in advance The Times story was not the only cause for animosity between the two candidates. After Peltola criticized Sullivan about the war in Iran, looking down at notes on her podium as she spoke, Sullivan turned to the moderators. “We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand were, we?” he asked. “No, sir,” one moderator said before another added: “Neither one of you got questions beforehand. Absolutely not.” “OK,” Sullivan said. “I’m just watching my opponent read from questions that seem to be answered.” “I’m prepared,” Peltola said. Sullivan appeared to back down from his suggestion while speaking with reporters after the debate, according to Alaska Public Media , which quoted him telling the hosts, “I’m not blaming you guys.” This story has been updated with additional information. item.title: The U.S. economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Yields are above multidecade highs , both gas and diesel prices continue to climb , and critical midterm elections are around the corner. Adding to pressure on the US economy and the current administration, the world's two largest hot wars are heating up. 'Iran knows when the midterms are too' In the Middle East, dual fronts along the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea have seen a resurgence of conflict in recent weeks that has heavily disrupted oil flows in the region. (Yasin Demirci/Anadolu via Getty Images) Anadolu via Getty Images Multiple tankers and container ships in the Strait of Hormuz either caught fire or sank this week in the Iran-dominated waterway. The Washington Institute has tracked more than two dozen attacks recorded since the start of the month. President Trump has said the US military won't resume airstrikes inside Iran before the midterm elections as White House negotiators continue angling for a diplomatic solution to the conflict now in its eighth month. Read more: How to protect your money as Mideast turmoil fuels market volatility Middle Eastern crude oil and petroleum product exports have declined significantly over the past week. (Murat Usubali/Anadolu via Getty Images) Anadolu via Getty Images At the same time, administration officials are reportedly war-gaming a major offensive to come after the November elections, when the president will be less encumbered by the political needs of the Republican Party. "The Trump Administration does not want Brent crude oil at $106/bbl going into the midterm elections, just a month away, and has said that he only plans to escalate offenses against Iran after the midterms are over, with what he hopes to be, a red wave," Rabobank cross-asset macro strategist Molly Schwartz said in a recent note to clients. To the west along the Red Sea, Yemen's Houthi militants have sharply escalated their campaign against the Saudi coalition opposing the group's bid for wider territorial control, launching multiple rounds of strikes on major airports inside the kingdom that have killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds. Houthi militants recently struck an office building belonging to the state-managed oil giant Saudi Aramco ( 2223.SR ). While the kingdom's oil production remains largely undisrupted, violent pestering by the Iran-allied Houthis is driving up oil prices . Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on Oct. 3, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images) - via Getty Images "Iran knows when the midterms are too," Schwartz added, "and if they want to further complicate Trump's plans, now is the perfect time to have the Houthis stir up trouble and make it increasingly difficult for the US to avoid intervening." Ukraine, Russia, and Starlink throttling Ukraine and Russia, which have been at war since Russia executed a stealth annexation of Crimea in 2014 and invaded its neighbor in February 2022, recently both escalated offensive strikes against critical infrastructure ahead of another winter. Kyiv leverages long-range drone attacks to knock out oil refineries inside Russia, claiming to have disrupted half the country's refining capacity, while Moscow has repeatedly targeted power plants and other civilian infrastructure inside Ukraine. Over the weekend, President Trump called for an "energy ceasefire," part of a bid to bring down US diesel prices that has included a deal that will see the US buy Russian fuel , breaking with several years of sanctions meant to pressure the Kremlin's war chest. Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery in Moscow following what the authorities said is a Ukrainian drone strike in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, on Sept., 20, 2026. (Reuters/Stringer/File Photo) Reuters / REUTERS Shortly after the announcement, Russia launched a round of strikes against power plants in Ukraine, prompting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to say Kyiv would continue to target Russian refineries. On Wednesday, Ukraine reported rate-throttling of Starlink , satellite communications services developed by SpaceX ( SPCX ), and its military subscription service StarShield. On Thursday evening, citing an official familiar with the matter, Reuters reported that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House." Ukrainian troops use both Starlink and Starshield terminals. (ISW) Oil prices and yields pressure US economy Taken together, the conflicts are putting immense pressure on the global energy system — and, increasingly, on the US economy. While oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to prewar levels via alternative routes, exports through the waterway itself — which before the war accounted for roughly one-fifth of global oil flows — have remained far below prewar levels. And prior to 2022, Russia provided roughly 10% of the world's diesel exports. But Moscow has largely been cut off from the market after international sanctions and domestic export bans. The US economy is feeling the disruption: Yields on US 10-year and 30-year Treasurys have climbed to levels not seen since the early 2000s, pressuring consumer and corporate borrowers. Gasoline and diesel prices have soared to record levels. Wednesday marked a record for the number of days in a year that gasoline stayed above $4 per gallon. Recent reports from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed inflation readings on both consumer and producer prices accelerating faster than expected , with energy prices rising at the quickest pace since March, just after the start of the Iran war. For the White House, those economic pressures have complicated the outlook for midterm elections less than three weeks away. In comments to reporters on Wednesday night, President Trump said again that the war in Iran will "end very soon," and the White House is reportedly considering the use of a GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) — the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, which would mark a major step-up in escalation. President Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15, 2026. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images) JIM WATSON via Getty Images Iran is not backing down : Parliamentary speaker Mohamed Bagher Ghalibaf said on Wednesday that Iran will fight until its demands are met in negotiations. In Ukraine, President Zelensky has ordered renewed attacks on Russian refineries . And with only a few short weeks left until the midterms, the reheating of both wars has left the White House — and, by proxy, the US economy — between a rock and a hard place. item.title: Trump's drug company holdings surged from $1.7 million to $56 million, Democrats say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Investments in pharmaceutical companies made on behalf of President Donald Trump increased significantly after he returned to the White House last year, with his portfolio adding millions of dollars in stock in firms that benefited from a Republican-backed law that shields certain medications from Medicare price negotiations, according to a report from congressional Democrats. The report, released Friday by the Joint Economic Committee’s minority arm, found that Trump’s pharmaceutical stock holdings grew from a maximum reported value of $1.7 million in 2024 to as much as $56.2 million at the end of 2025. The report said that included up to $39.1 million worth of stock held in companies that benefited from exemptions to Medicare’s drug price negotiation program, which came through a provision in Republicans' 2025 tax and spending law . Additional analysis of Trump's financial disclosures provided by committee Democrats showed that his investment portfolio bought as much as $2.55 million in shares of pharmaceutical companies benefiting from the exemptions on three dates before he signed the legislation in July 2025. That included up to $950,000 in purchases on July 1, 2025, the day the Senate passed the bill . His portfolio also bought as much as $1 million in AbbVie stock in August 2025, after the bill became law. The Republican president’s wealth has grown since he took office last year through a web of business interests , many of which have benefited from the policy moves of his administration. The White House has repeatedly denied any ethics issues and accused Democrats of “attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest.” The report also noted that the exemptions policy could leave some Medicare beneficiaries paying thousands of dollars more for certain cancer treatments and other medications than they would have if Medicare had been allowed to negotiate lower prices. The findings come as Trump has made lowering prescription drug costs a central part of his healthcare policy, striking deals with pharmaceutical companies that his administration says will make medications more affordable for Americans, although drug pricing is based on a complicated set of factors . Recent polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that most Americans think Trump is profiting off the presidency in unethical or illegal ways and is focused more on his wealth than on helping people like them. Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who leads the Joint Economic Committee’s minority arm, called the report’s findings “outrageous and yet typical from this president, who makes the American people foot the bill again and again for his own gains.” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. He denied any conflict of interest. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said in a statement. A law from President Joe Biden's Democratic administration allowed Medicare for the first time to negotiate prices for some of the costliest prescription drugs. Republicans' 2025 tax and spending bill expanded an existing exemption for medications developed to treat rare diseases or conditions, delaying when certain costly drugs could become eligible for negotiations or excluding them entirely, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Also known as the orphan drug exclusion, the carveout allows drug companies to continue charging lucrative prices that might otherwise have been reduced through Medicare negotiations. Supporters of the change argued that a broader exemption would encourage drug companies to develop treatments for rare diseases. Critics say it allows makers of blockbuster medications to avoid negotiations that could lower costs for Medicare and its recipients. The report estimated that Medicare beneficiaries receiving the cancer drugs Keytruda, manufactured by Merck, and Opdivo, by Bristol Myers Squibb, could pay roughly $5,000 more annually than they would if Medicare negotiated prices for the medications. Trump's portfolio includes stock in both firms. The report also said that Trump's portfolio continued to buy and sell pharma company stocks throughout the first eight months of 2026, adding as much as $3.5 million in stock wealth in the sector. All recent U.S. presidents have dumped their stocks before assuming office, put their money in broadly diversified funds or set up a “blind” trust so they couldn’t even know what they owned. Trump has put his broader business interests in a trust managed by his sons. But the arrangement rejects the conflict of interest protections that his recent predecessors in office had instituted. ___ Associated Press writer Bernard Condon in New York contributed to this report. (Archive Photos) Former Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger walked free from prison Friday morning after serving seven years behind bars for the murder of Botham Jean. Guyger, 38, shot 26-year-old Jean inside his apartment in September 2018. He had been sitting on his couch eating ice cream when Guyger, who was off-duty but still in uniform, opened the door. She said she mistook Jean’s apartment for her own and believed he was a burglar. He lived on the fourth floor; she lived on the third. She was found guilty of murder and sentenced to 10 years in prison, but was granted parole earlier this month. Guyger was released after 10 a.m. from the Christina Melton Crain Unit in Gatesville. CBS reported live from the unit, but news cameras didn’t capture her release. Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials said Guyger was released into community supervision. Guyger was required to travel directly to her new residence and check in immediately with her parole officer, according to Texas parole requirements . She was allowed to take home personal items accumulated while in prison and will either wear state-issued civilian clothes or clothes brought to her by visitors or the people picking her up. Guyger walked out with her parole papers, a temporary ID and a prepaid debit card or check for money left in her inmate trust account. Guyger was denied parole in 2024 after the state parole board said she was not rehabilitated or ready for release. Her request was granted this time after a review found her record showed no documented pattern of violence, that she maintained a “satisfactory institutional adjustment” and that she completed a treatment plan that “should enhance” her chances of obtaining — and keeping — a full-time job, a Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles spokesperson said in early October. The board has several options for what type of parole to grant an inmate, a vote that depends on individual circumstances and the inmate’s behavior during time served. Guyger was granted direct release with no additional restrictions beyond her parole conditions, the least restrictive form of parole approval a Texas inmate can receive. The decision to release her sparked a new wave of interest and emotion around the case, which drew international attention, sparked protests and led Texas lawmakers to pass the Botham Jean Act. Also known as Bo’s Law, the statute requires officers to keep their body cameras on for the entirety of their participation in an investigation. That same year, Dallas renamed part of South Lamar Street for Jean. “The past eight years have been an incredibly traumatic and painful experience for Botham Jean’s family,” the family said in an official statement released in early October. “The loss of Botham has left our family forever dismembered, and that is something we continue to live with every day.” A large photo of Botham Jean is displayed with photos and cards on one of the tables in his childhood home in Castries, St. Lucia on Sept. 25, 2018. Botham Jean was shot and killed in his apartment by off-duty Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger. (Vernon Bryant/Staff Photographer) Guyger’s parole conditions were not released, but her trial attorney, who no longer represents her, told The Dallas Morning News after the parole vote that she has a job that will keep her out of the public life and a living arrangement that will stay private. “She’s hopeful, optimistic, tremendously remorseful,” attorney Robert Rogers said. “That’s probably something she’ll always live with.” Parole conditions Most parolees must follow the same basic set of rules, alongside any special conditions decided by the parole board, which are typically kept confidential. Guyger will have to follow her parole conditions until September 2029. Failure to follow the conditions can result in parole revocation, which sends the inmate back to prison for the remainder of their sentence, or lesser sanctions such as curfew adjustments or brief incarceration in a facility designed for parolees. State law requires all parolees to get permission from their parole officer if they want to change residences or leave the state. They must be working or in school, and they have to check in regularly with their parole officer, submit monthly education or work reports, and submit to random alcohol and drug testing and unannounced searches. They’re forbidden from breaking the law, owning or being around firearms and ammunition, and from contacting the victim directly or indirectly. They must make restitution payments and reimburse the prison for some educational programs. Guyger still faces a judgment of nearly $100 million from a federal civil suit connected to Jean’s murder. item.title: Photos show Pope Leo celebrating Mass at the hospital after cancer surgery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Vatican released new photos of Pope Leo XIV — the first since his lung cancer surgery — showing him celebrating Mass at the hospital in Rome. The photos, released Friday, show the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that the pontiff presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily. In his homily, Leo thanked the medical personnel for their service and their closeness to those who are fragile, and for the way they have taken care of him. The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week . He is expected to remain at Gemelli Hospital until Oct. 20. On Thursday, he resumed "a little bit of work activity, " including reading documents, and co-celebrated Mass, Vatican officials said. He also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state. Doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement" in his recovery. "His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Leo's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. The Vatican said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine . Leo also called for a ceasefire to allow for food and medical assistance to be distributed in the region, as well as the safe evacuation of civilians. "The Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See's commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," the Vatican said. The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The Vatican said Leo will make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer. Past popes who have been hospitalized have recited the Angelus from the balcony on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital. Trip to South America appears still on Leo is scheduled to travel to South America next month. His ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time. However, on Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the pope's plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Posting the media list signaled that, at least organizationally, the trip was going ahead. Cancer patients send well-wishing notes to Leo The Vatican also released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli's pediatric oncology ward. One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. "My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon," he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom. Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language. "When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we're going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you," she wrote. "I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/photos-pope-leo-mass-hospital-recovery-surgery/

item.title: Trump officials scrutinized Omar in 2019. They didn't find citizenship issues.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Seven years ago, a political appointee in the first Trump administration approached U.S. immigration authorities with a request that alarmed career staffers: Scrub the immigration records of Rep. Ilhan Omar, then a newly elected Democratic lawmaker from Minnesota, for evidence of fraud. That 2019 demand, detailed by three former immigration officials, struck staffers at the time as a highly unusual effort to wield federal power to dig up compromising material on a sitting member of Congress who was a prominent critic of President Donald Trump. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The request sparked a swift review examining Omar's history, her family's past as Somali refugees resettled in the United States and rumors that had circulated for years in conservative media over her marriage. Homeland Security Investigations - the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement - ultimately determined there was insufficient evidence of wrongdoing, one of the former officials said. The idea of pursuing a full investigation was eventually abandoned. Now, though, with Trump back in the White House and his administration using federal power to take aim at perceived enemies, Omar has once again found herself in federal crosshairs. She is now facing an inquiry over some of the same allegations investigators previously deemed not worth pursuing. The current effort - which burst into public view Monday as federal agents descended upon Omar's D.C. home - is focused on whether she or her father lied on paperwork they submitted to obtain legal status and eventual citizenship after arriving in the U.S. in the 1990s. Investigators are reexamining questions about Omar's birthdate and her late father's past military history in Somalia, which had passed scrutiny during the 2019 review. Depending on their findings, the administration could seek to charge Omar with a crime or move to challenge her status in the country. But such a step would be a sharp reversal of the earlier review, which found no issue with her naturalization, one of the former officials familiar with the earlier effort said. "I think her citizenship is solid and there wasn't any fraud there," the ex-official said. Omar has dismissed the revived investigation as yet another example of the Justice Department, under Trump, attempting "to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." "Trump has spread lie after lie about the Congresswoman in a desperate attempt to justify his extraordinary abuse of power," her spokesperson said in a statement Thursday. "This is politically motivated and an escalation of Trump's personal vendetta against her lasting over a decade." This account of the Trump administration's current and past efforts to investigate and possibly build a case against Omar is based on interviews with a dozen people, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss nonpublic details of those probes. Several current and former officials raised questions about the scope, tactics and motivations driving the current Omar investigation, which they say appears to be disregarding key norms on how immigration reviews are typically handled and bypassing guardrails intended to ensure federal inquiries, including those looking into sitting lawmakers, are not perceived to be driven by politics. A spokesperson for the Justice Department said the agency does not comment on ongoing investigations. The Department of Homeland Security referred questions to the Justice Department. Questions about the probe came into play ahead of this week's highly public search of Omar's home. Before carrying out the search, prosecutors spent days working to allay concerns from a federal judge that their plans could run afoul of constitutional protections shielding members of Congress from unwarranted executive branch intrusion, according to three people familiar with the matter. U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh, who ultimately signed off on the warrant, first imposed strict conditions on how the search should be carried out, the people said. His limits on the search appeared intended to ensure that the warrant fell in line with the D.C. court's interpretation of the Constitution's speech and debate clause, which generally shields lawmakers' legislative duties and actions from criminal probes. As part of the search, agents removed boxes of documents and seized Omar's cellphone and passport, one person familiar with the matter said. Trump has assailed Omar for years, and this week condemned her again on social media and public remarks. "I think she's a terrible person," he told reporters. "But that's really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it." Trump's administration has also made clear its scrutiny on Omar is not limited to immigration issues. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in D.C., announced Tuesday her office had launched its own investigation into Omar's personal finances, tied to disclosure statements she filed in Congress last year and separate from the immigration probe. Pirro, a former Fox News host, once drew a highly unusual public rebuke from the network in 2019 for on-air comments suggesting that Omar, as a Muslim, could not be loyal to the U.S. Constitution. Omar's office has previously dismissed questions raised by House Republicans over her financial disclosure statements as a right-wing attempt to "manufacture controversy." However, federal prosecutors' interest in the finances of Omar extend back to the Biden administration, according to two people familiar with the effort. Those individuals said it was not clear why the investigation during the prior administration appeared to have stalled. But the revived immigration investigation into Omar appears to be the furthest along and the administration's higher priority. Alessandra P. Serano, an associate deputy attorney general who is playing a key role in the probe, went before the judge seeking the search warrant for Omar's home, two people familiar with the matter said. Attorney General Todd Blanche also recently dispatched Serano, a trusted aide, to Florida to check in on the high-profile and struggling Florida-based investigation into former Obama and Biden-era officials, according to multiple people. Authorities have issued more than a dozen subpoenas related to Omar and the investigation into her, including some to her siblings, seeking testimony before a grand jury in Minneapolis in the coming weeks, two people said. The Washington Post has reported that investigators are focused on whether Omar or her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, intentionally misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him as a minor when he was naturalized in 2000. Investigators are also scrutinizing whether Omar's father may have purposefully lied or omitted information on his past military service in Somalia that could have made him ineligible to obtain legal status in the country. But three former officials involved in the 2019 review of Omar's immigration file said both of those issues were considered during that inquiry. An official with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, who was normally tasked with scrutinizing the backgrounds of people including serious criminals, terrorists and potential national security threats, was asked in 2019 to review Omar's background. The then-freshman lawmaker had emerged as a frequent focus of conservative attacks. At the time, the agency was primarily focused on possible fraud related to Omar's marriage to her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Right-wing commentators had repeatedly pressed unsubstantiated claims that Omar and Elmi were siblings who carried out a sham marriage so that Elmi could obtain U.S. immigration benefits. Elmi had previously filed an immigration petition related to his marriage-based green card that would move it from conditional status to permanent. USCIS requested additional evidence due to concerns over the validity of his marriage, but Elmi withdrew the application following that request, one of the former officials said. Elmi could not immediately be reached for comment Thursday. The 2019 review of Omar also looked at other issues, some of which are being examined anew. For instance, back then, USCIS quickly determined it could not accurately answer questions over Omar's age because refugees frequently come from countries with little or no birth records, making it hard to determine with any certainty. "That's not strange and that's not a red flag to me," one of the former officials said. "It's just very, very common that there aren't great birth records." The agency also examined Omar's father's immigration file but did not find any issues, according to the former official. The USCIS officer tasked with vetting Omar produced a one-page memo of those findings and shared it with a senior USCIS official and a fraud detention official before the effort was ultimately abandoned, the person said. Due to the sensitivity, the memo was printed out, and distributed in person, and not shared over email. Whether the current investigation will uncover more substantial evidence to back the administration's fraud claims remains to be seen. Even if the Trump administration finds wrongdoing, any attempt to strip her citizenship would likely be lengthy and result in a legal battle. The administration, however, is also exploring the possibility that it could seek to revoke her citizenship certificate if the current investigation does not result in criminal charges or a conviction, a senior Trump administration official said. Revocation is a rarely employed USCIS administrative process that can be used to cancel the document due to fraud or an error. The process is not restricted to a certain period of time like criminal denaturalizations, which are subject to a 10-year statute of limitations. The revocation would not remove her citizenship but would make it challenging to obtain some government documents. This action could open the door to immigration-related charges and possibly removal proceedings, though such a novel application of the administrative authority would almost certainly face challenges from Omar in court. In a statement, Omar's spokesperson assailed the Trump administration's efforts to target the congresswoman. "He has lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country," the statement read. "But the truth is that Trump's push to strip her of her citizenship and deport her has no basis in the law and has no precedent. This isn't a legitimate law enforcement action." Alexei Koseff contributed to this report. item.title: Oregon governor praises 'heroic' bystander who stopped school shooter
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A teenager shot his way through locked doors at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher, police say. The children were 5, 8 and 11 years old, Bend Police Department Chief Mike Krantz said during a press conference on Thursday evening. The suspect, identified as a 16-year-old Bend resident, was shot and killed inside the school by a member of the community who saw him enter the building and pursued him, Krantz said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were also sent to a hospital with critical injuries. The Associated Press on Friday identified the bystander who killed the shooter as Kyle Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident and the father of two young daughters at the school. "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, said while reading a prepared statement to reporters outside her son's home near the school. President Trump on Friday called Giamanco a “great hero” who prevented the attack from being “much worse.” “Thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” he said. On Thursday, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised the previously anonymous bystander for "heroically" intervening and stopping further loss of life. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," Kotek said. Police did not release the names of the victims or the shooter. Krantz did not say what kind of gun the suspect used, although a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told the Associated Press that it was a pump-action shotgun. Multiple outlets have reported that the shotgun was originally purchased by the shooter's mother, citing law enforcement sources. It was not immediately clear if the shooter knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended. Police haven't released any information about the shooter's potential motive. "This is going to be a long investigation," Krantz said. "We will have a large police presence at Silver Rail Elementary School for the next several days as our officers continue to conduct a very thorough investigation so we get all the answers. We appreciate your patience as we continue to investigate this terrible tragedy." The Bend Police Department has said it will provide further information at a press conference on Friday afternoon. How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. item.title: Katie Zacharia reportedly out as White House press secretary after first week on the job
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump signaled on Friday that he might replace embattled new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after less than one week on the job. Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News and the Washington Post published similar reports. If confirmed, that would make Zacharia the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. "We're talking about doing something," Trump told reporters outside the White House, adding that he told Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 Trump said he would discuss the matter further with Zacharia when he returns from a Friday campaign rally in Georgia. The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, she has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confimed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . "Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" "When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law." What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." item.title: Body found in barrel at Lake Mead identified as 1980s shooting victim
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The remains of a man who was shot in the head and stuffed into a rusted barrel found on the shore of Lake Mead after the water level dropped were identified Thursday as an Arkansas man whose decades-old killing remains unsolved. Edward Lelburian Jackson was in his mid- to late 50s when he died, Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse said. Authorities are looking for people to come forward to help solve Jackson's killing. There was no evidence directly linking the killing to organized crime in nearby Las Vegas despite longstanding speculation, although a connection hasn't been ruled out, police said. An expert on mob activity in the city said the case bears the "earmarks" of a mob hit and that questions still linger. The discovery sparked memories of Las Vegas' mob era Jackson was identified with the help of a bone sample sent for genealogy profiling, along with three angles of a composite face and clothing Jackson was wearing when he died, Rouse said. "We were able to confirm that the remains were in fact Edward Jackson," she said. The discovery of the barrel by boaters in May 2022 sparked memories of the city's mob era , which lasted from the 1940s to the mid-1980s. Organized crime helped build up Las Vegas, and a body stuffed in a barrel was known to signify a mob killing. Jackson, believed to be from Hot Springs, Arkansas, had a brief criminal history in the early 1980s in Salt Lake City, Utah, which included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud, said Robert Price, a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department homicide lieutenant. Police said Jackson was married for a short time with no known children, CBS affiliate KLAS-TV reported . It's unclear why Jackson was in Las Vegas Price said there is nothing to tie the killing to organized crime. He added, however, that it hasn't been ruled out. Jackson's family told investigators that he liked to travel and detectives found records of him in California, where he lived with his wife in the early '70s. His family said they last saw him in Arkansas in the early '80s, and it is unclear why he was in Las Vegas. Homicide detectives will continue working to figure out what happened to him, said Price. "It's an unsolved case. It will never be closed until we solve it," Price said Thursday. "I would say that this is a piece of the puzzle and as we get more and more pieces, we'll be able to keep on digging deeper." Authorities had already said the man was shot, and they estimate he was killed in the early 1980s. Jackson had not been reported missing The man had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes. Price said the family didn't report him missing. "They knew that he had traveled the country, would show up when he showed up, just to say hi. But they didn't think anything other than that. They just figured he was out and about," he said. Researcher says case has all the "earmarks of a mob hit" Geoff Schumacher, vice president of research, collections and programs at The Mob Museum in Las Vegas, said there are still many questions about who Jackson was and what he was involved in that "earned him a trip in a barrel into the lake." Members of organized crime were involved in the Las Vegas casino industry from the 1940s to the mid-1980s, both behind the scenes and through shadow ownerships of casinos, Schumacher said. He said the case had all the "earmarks of a mob hit," mirroring another case from 1976 when Italian mobster John Roselli was killed and stuffed in a barrel and dumped into a bay outside of Miami Beach. Schumacher said he and Mob Museum staff will comb their records to try to help solve the case. "I think this story is not over," he said. Other bodies discovered as Lake Mead recedes Las Vegas historian Michael Green said whoever committed the crime probably thought the body would "never come near the surface." In the early 1980s, the lake levels were so high that the spillways flooded at Hoover Dam, he said. Now, Lake Mead is at a historic low due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater. In August, the water level dipped to 1,039.77 feet above sea level, according to the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation , well below the previous record low set in July 2022. Several other sets of remains were found at Lake Mead in 2022. Another set of skeletal remains was discovered that May, and they were identified as a drowning victim from 2002. Skeletal remains found in August were identified as a 52-year-old Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1998. The remains of another drowning victim, Donald Smith, who was believed to have drowned in 1974 , were found in October 2022. Its receding waters are leaving behind the usual flotsam and jetsam of a lake heavily trafficked by weekend boaters — and even exposing a ship dating back to World War II. Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the U.S., part of a system that provides Colorado River water to people across the U.S. Southwest and Mexico. In 2022, Lake Mead's dropping level exposed Las Vegas' uppermost drinking water intake. That forced authorities to switch to a deeper intake to keep serving the city's 2.4 million residents. Survivors of the 2009 Fort Hood massacre praised President Donald Trump's decision not to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, after warning that broadcasting his death could turn the execution into a spectacle and hand terrorist groups a propaganda tool. Hasan is still set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, 2026, and Trump said the immediate families of his victims will be permitted to witness the execution in person. But it will no longer be broadcast to the general public as previously announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. "It proves that we are a better people, a better nation, and that we're not barbaric," Lunsford said in immediate reaction to the walk-back by Trump on Thursday. "We don't glorify such actions." Veteran Shot 7 Times In Fort Hood Massacre Has A Warning For Americans Planning To Watch Execution Lunsford said he supports Hasan's death sentence and execution by firing squad but drew a line at broadcasting it to the public. Read On The Fox News App "For it to be made a spectacle for everyone to witness how they're gonna do a tailgate or, 'Hey, we're gonna have a cookout and we're gonna watch this man be put to death.' No, it's not about that," Lunsford said. "It's not a spectacle. It's not a pay-per-view event or a WWE wrestling match or even a boxing match." He also warned that footage of Hasan's execution could be seized upon by terrorist organizations.
